g12-history-uh7-t1.overview: This lesson explains how European colonial rule ended in Africa, contrasting the relatively peaceful road to independence in West Africa with the bloody war in Algeria, and reviewing the economic legacy the new states inherited.
objectives: Explain why independence came with relative ease in West Africa
Describe how Ghana, Nigeria, Sierra Leone and Gambia won independence
Evaluate the 1958 referendum of Charles de Gaulle in French West Africa
Trace the course of the Algerian War of Independence from 1954 to 1962
Assess the economic and social impact of colonialism on the new states
g12-history-uh7-t1.simple: Independence in Africa came by two roads: peaceful and armed. In West Africa there were few white settlers and the nationalist movements had long experience, so independence was won with relative ease. Under capable leaders like Nkrumah and Azikiwe, the Gold Coast became Ghana in March 1957, Nigeria in October 1960, Sierra Leone in April 1961 and Gambia in February 1964. In French West Africa, General de Gaulle's 1958 referendum offered autonomy within the French Community or immediate independence without French aid; only Guinea voted no, and by November 1960 all French West African colonies were independent. Because about one million white settlers lived in Algeria, its war of independence from 1954 to 1962 was among the bloodiest, ending with the Evian Agreement of 1962.
g12-history-uh7-t1.detailed:
Two roads to independence. The national liberation movements in Africa took two courses, violent and non-violent. In West Africa independence was achieved with relative ease because there was no significant number of white settlers and the nationalist movements had a long history and better experience of providing leadership. Nationalist agitation was strongest in the Gold Coast and Nigeria, led by two very capable men, Nnamdi Azikiwe of Nigeria and Kwame Nkrumah of the Gold Coast, both educated in the USA. Bitter clashes marked the years from 1945 to 1954, with Gold Coast nationalists accusing British officials of using talk of training Africans to keep colonial rule alive. The Gold Coast became independent in March 1957 under the new name Ghana; Nigeria followed in October 1960, Sierra Leone in April 1961 and Gambia in February 1964.

French West Africa reforms. After the Second World War France realized it must grant more rights to its colonial peoples, but at first it wanted association rather than full independence. Each colony was allowed to elect a territorial assembly, a real advance, yet the colonies were given no legislative power: the laws for each were still promulgated by the French Minister of Colonies in Paris. Radical nationalists therefore began to demand unconditional full independence.

The referendum of 1958. In 1958 General Charles de Gaulle became French President and issued a new constitution transforming the French Union into a French Community. Each colony had to choose in a referendum between voting yes and becoming an autonomous republic within the Community, or voting no and becoming immediately independent without French economic and technical assistance. Because their economies were highly dependent on France, almost all colonies voted yes. Only Guinea voted no and became fully independent in 1958; France immediately recalled its professionals and stopped assistance, and Sekou Toure, Guinea's first president, turned to the U.S.S.R. for support. By November 1960 all the colonies of French West Africa had achieved full independence. The year 1960 is known as 'Africa Year' because seventeen French colonies became independent in it. Except for Guinea, they maintained close ties with France.

Algeria: the settler problem. In colonies with many white settlers the colonial powers refused to grant independence easily. Algeria, a French colony since 1830, was administered as part of France itself, and about one million white settlers, the colons, considered it part of France. Even Algerian elite figures like Ferhat Abbas at first accepted this, but they later demanded independence. The war began in November 1954, led mainly by former soldiers of the French army and Algerians of peasant origin. Ben Bella formed the Revolutionary Committee for Unity and Action, later renamed the National Liberation Front (FLN), which by 1956 was a highly organized fighting force funded by Egypt, Morocco, Tunisia and the Arab League.

The end of the war. The prolonged war shook France itself: the fall of the French Fourth Republic was related to Algeria, and the crisis returned de Gaulle to power in May 1958. In 1959 he offered integration with France, absolute independence, or independence in cooperation with France. The FLN demanded absolute independence, and in 1960 the colons and some French generals, organized in a terrorist Secret Army, even tried to overthrow de Gaulle. On March 18, 1962 France and the FLN signed the Evian Agreement, and Algeria became independent on July 1, 1962, with Ben Bella as its first president.

The colonial legacy. The new states inherited an underdeveloped economy. Colonialism was a double-edged sword: it built some roads and railroads, but mainly to exploit resources, as in northern Nigeria and the mineral spur lines of Sierra Leone. It disarticulated African production, markets and trade, made trade export-import oriented, prematurely integrated Africa into the world market, and left no organic link between agriculture and industry, so the surplus profits were never reinvested in Africa.

keyTerms.def: Colonialism in which a large European settler population lives permanently in the colony, making peaceful decolonization much harder.
The name for the white settlers of Algeria, about one million by 1960, who considered Algeria part of France.
The 1958 structure proposed by de Gaulle in which colonies voting 'Yes' became autonomous republics tied to France.
The Algerian independence movement created from Ben Bella's Revolutionary Committee for Unity and Action; it fought France from 1954 to 1962.
The accord of March 18, 1962 between France and the FLN that ended the Algerian war of independence.
The year 1960, when seventeen French colonies in Africa achieved independence.
Leader of Guinea, the only French West African colony to vote 'No' in 1958 and choose immediate independence.
The colonial breaking apart of African production, markets, trade and transport so that each part served Europe, not Africa's own development.

workedExamples.problem: Historians ask why independence was peaceful in Ghana but violent in Algeria. Using the settler-factor framework, explain the difference.
workedExamples.given: West Africa had no significant number of white settlers; Algeria had about one million colons by 1960 who considered Algeria part of France.
workedExamples.formula: Framework: the presence or absence of white settlers decides whether decolonization is negotiated or fought.
workedExamples.substitution: Without settlers, Britain could transfer power to experienced nationalists like Azikiwe and Nkrumah; with settlers, France fought a war to defend their position.
workedExamples.calculation: The settler block made negotiation impossible in Algeria, while its absence in West Africa allowed calm transfer of power.
workedExamples.answer: Settler colonialism, not African determination alone, explains why Algeria's liberation was a bloody war and Ghana's was a peaceful march to independence in 1957.

workedExamples.problem: Interpret the 1958 referendum result in French West Africa. What does the 'Yes' vote tell a historian?
workedExamples.given: De Gaulle warned that a 'No' vote meant losing French economic and technical assistance; almost all colonies voted 'Yes'; only Guinea voted 'No'.
workedExamples.formula: Framework: the referendum measures economic dependence, not political preference.
workedExamples.substitution: The colonies' economies were highly dependent on French assistance, so autonomy seemed safer than a risky break with France.
workedExamples.calculation: Freedom without funds looked dangerous; Guinea gambled on 'No' and survived because the U.S.S.R. filled the gap France left.
workedExamples.answer: The referendum shows neo-colonial dependence: the colonies chose attached autonomy because independence threatened their economies, which is why Guinea alone became fully independent in 1958.

workedExamples.problem: Connect the Algerian war with the political crisis inside France. What is the cause-and-effect chain?
workedExamples.given: The Algerian War of Independence began in November 1954; the French Fourth Republic fell; de Gaulle returned in May 1958; the Secret Army attempted to overthrow him in 1960.
workedExamples.formula: Concept: a colonial war can destabilize the metropolitan government that fights it.
workedExamples.substitution: Prolonged war against the FLN discredited the Fourth Republic, brought de Gaulle to power, and provoked settler rebellion against de Gaulle himself.
workedExamples.calculation: War abroad created crisis at home; crisis produced new policy; the 1959 alternatives and negotiations ended with the Evian Agreement of 1962.
workedExamples.answer: The Algerian war was both a liberation struggle and a metropolitan crisis that toppled the Fourth Republic and finally forced France to negotiate independence.

commonMistakes: Thinking all of Africa won independence peacefully; the nature of struggle depended on the presence of white settlers.
Confusing the Gold Coast with Ghana as different territories; the Gold Coast became Ghana at independence in 1957.
Believing the 1958 referendum gave immediate independence to most colonies; it created only autonomous republics within the French Community.
Assuming France welcomed Guinea's independence; France withdrew all professionals and assistance, and Sekou Toure had to turn to the Soviets.
Thinking Algeria was ruled as a distant colony; France administered it as part of France, which strengthened the settlers' resistance.
Dating the Algerian war from the Evian Agreement; the war began in November 1954 and ended in 1962.
Attributing independence only to wartime exhaustion; capable nationalist leadership such as Azikiwe and Nkrumah was decisive.
applications: Explaining how Ethiopia's victory over Italy at Adwa in 1896 inspired Africans still fighting for independence in the 1950s and 1960s.
Using the settler-settler framework to compare liberation struggles in Zimbabwe and Angola with the peaceful case of Nigeria.
Tracing how dependence, like Franco-African ties after 1960, explains why political flags alone do not end foreign control.
Analysing advice given to a newly freed colony: what Guinea learned in 1958 about preparing before cutting dependency.
Debating in class whether de Gaulle's referendum was decolonization or a device to preserve French influence.
g12-history-uh7-t1.summary: Independence came peacefully where there were few settlers, as in Ghana (1957), Nigeria (1960), Sierra Leone (1961) and Gambia (1964), but violently where settlers resisted, above all in Algeria from 1954 to 1962. The 1958 referendum offered only attached autonomy, which all colonies but Guinea accepted, and seventeen more states became free in 1960, 'Africa Year'. The new states inherited an underdeveloped, export-oriented economy designed by colonialism for Europe's benefit.

g12-history-uh7-t2.overview: This lesson examines political instability in independent Africa: the wave of military coups of the 1960s to 1980s, why the armies intervened, and the contrasting cases of Nigeria and Ghana.
objectives: Explain why military coups became the most frequent means of changing governments in Africa
Identify the countries that suffered coups and counter-coups in the 1960s and 1970s
Assess the corrupt and tyrannical regimes that fell in 1979
Trace the political crisis and civil war of Nigeria from 1964 to 1979
Analyse the chain of coups and reforms in Ghana from 1966 to 1981
g12-history-uh7-t2.simple: After independence many African states lost political stability and fell under military rule. Colonial armies had been kept for internal control, not national defense, and at independence they saw civil politics as an open field. Most French-speaking states, except Guinea, Senegal and Cote d'Ivoire, went over to military rule in the 1960s, and by the 1970s and 1980s the coup d'etat was the most frequent means of changing government. Coups were at first welcomed as a cure for inefficient and corrupt civilian regimes, but military rulers proved just as likely to be corrupt and tyrannical. Nigeria went through a rigged election, two coups of 1966, the Biafra civil war of 1967-70 and reforms to civilian rule by 1979; Ghana saw the fall of Nkrumah in 1966 and Rawlings' return in 1981.
g12-history-uh7-t2.detailed:
Why armies stepped in. Apart from the two world wars, colonial African armies were mainly held in reserve for internal use against potential rebellious subjects, not for defense against hostile neighbors. At independence they had little real role, and when civilian governments failed, the military saw itself as an alternative. An interesting exception was the Seychelles, which had no army at all: its prime minister seized power with only a handful of colleagues, and only afterwards did the government need an army to guard against counter-coups.

The coup wave. From the 1960s, the major problem in many African countries was a lack of political stability. Most French-speaking states, with the notable exception of Guinea, Senegal and Cote d'Ivoire, went over to military rule during the 1960s, while Togo and Dahomey (today's Benin) suffered frequent coups and counter-coups; between 1963 and 1969 five violent changes of government occurred in Dahomey alone. From November 1965 coup followed coup, taking Nigeria and Ghana in early 1966. In this period we can mention the coup in Congo Brazzaville of August 1963, the Algerian coup of June 1965, three coups in Libya, Sudan and Somalia in 1969, and the coup in Uganda in 1971. Coup d'etat remained the most frequent means of changing government throughout the 1970s and 1980s.

Welcome, then disappointment. African coups were apparently reactions to inefficient and corrupt civilian regimes, so most were initially welcomed: the military was believed to be disciplined and free from corruption. But this did not mean the military was a positive for development; military rulers were just as likely to be corrupt and tyrannical as civilian ones. The years around 1979 saw the downfall of three of Africa's most corrupt and tyrannical regimes: General Jean-Bedel Bokassa of the Central African Republic (1966-79), Field Marshal Idi Amin Dada of Uganda (1971-79), and Francisco Macias Nguema of Equatorial Guinea (1968-79). Amin and Nguema were responsible for the torture and deaths of thousands of opponents, and Amin's regime looted and destroyed what had been one of Africa's most thriving agriculturally based economies. In September 1962 the President of Togo had narrowly escaped an attempted assassination, showing how exposed leaders were.

Nigeria: from rigged elections to civil war. In Nigeria the widespread belief that the elections of 1964-65 had been rigged destroyed the credibility of the civilian government. The first army coup of January 1966 was followed by another in July amid fears of ethnic domination by Igbo Southerners or Hausa Northerners. The massacre of 20,000 Igbo people living in the northern region led directly to the Biafra secession and the civil war of 1967-70. General Gowon, who had seized power in the counter-coup of 1966, steered Nigeria through this inheritance and achieved a remarkable post-war reconciliation, though his government later grew inefficient. He was overthrown by General Murtala Muhammed in July 1975, who restored moral authority, began serious reforms and set a timetable for a return to civilian rule in 1979; Muhammed was assassinated in February 1976 by envious middle-ranking officers, and General Obasanjo completed the reforms and returned Nigeria to civilian rule in 1979.

Ghana: cycles of coup and reform. Corruption, extravagant spending and intolerance of criticism, plus specific military grievances, led to the overthrow of Kwame Nkrumah in February 1966; he was blamed for giving priority to external affairs while ignoring Ghana's economic problems, and was exiled in Guinea. The civilian government of Dr Kofi A. Busia could not solve the economic crisis in the face of a sharp fall in the world price of cocoa, so Colonel Ignatius Acheampong seized power in 1972. His noted achievement, 'Operation Feed Yourself', aimed to reduce dependence on expensive food imports, but Ghana was hit hard by the huge oil price rise of 1973-74. Flight Lieutenant Jerry Rawlings seized power in 1979, executed three former military heads of state for corrupt practices, and returned the country to civilian rule within three months; dissatisfied again, he seized power in December 1981, proclaiming a 'people's revolution' and removing the old elites.

keyTerms.def: The sudden seizure of government by the military; the most frequent means of changing government in Africa throughout the 1970s and 1980s.
A second coup that reverses or replaces the military rulers of an earlier coup, as in Nigeria in July 1966.
The secessionist state declared by the Igbo after the massacres of 1966, whose breakaway caused the Nigerian civil war of 1967-70.
Acheampong's Ghanaian programme aimed at reducing dependence on expensive food imports.
Gowon's remarkably humane treatment of Biafrans after the Nigerian civil war of 1967-70.
A government marked by corruption and cruelty toward its own people, like those of Bokassa, Idi Amin and Macias Nguema.
A system of ideas, such as capitalism or socialism, that can divide African states and block united action.

workedExamples.problem: Explain, step by step, how Nigeria moved from rigged elections to civil war.
workedExamples.given: Elections of 1964-65 believed to be rigged; coups of January and July 1966; massacre of 20,000 Igbo in the northern region.
workedExamples.formula: Framework: political crisis deepens in cause-and-effect chains: disputed election, coup, ethnic massacre, secession, war.
workedExamples.substitution: The rigged vote destroyed confidence in civilian rule; the coups removed it; the Igbo massacre produced the Biafra secession.
workedExamples.calculation: Each stage removed another peaceful option, so war followed almost logically in 1967.
workedExamples.answer: Nigeria's slide shows how a disputed election escalated through military intervention and ethnic massacre into the Biafra war of 1967-70.

workedExamples.problem: A classmate argues that coups were good for Africa because people welcomed them. Evaluate this using the textbook evidence.
workedExamples.given: Coups were initially welcomed against corrupt civilian regimes, yet Bokassa, Idi Amin and Macias Nguema ruled corruptly and tyrannically, and Amin destroyed a thriving agricultural economy.
workedExamples.formula: Framework: judge a regime by performance in power, not by promises before taking power.
workedExamples.substitution: The welcome given to the first coups does not fix the record of military rule afterwards.
workedExamples.calculation: Since military rulers were just as likely to be corrupt and tyrannical as civilian ones, the argument collapses on the evidence of 1979's fallen tyrants.
workedExamples.answer: The welcome was a hope, not a result: military rule often reproduced, or worsened, the corruption it claimed to cure.

workedExamples.problem: Compare the paths of Nigeria and Ghana back to civilian rule after coups.
workedExamples.given: Nigeria: Murtala Muhammed's 1975 reforms, timetable for 1979, assassination in 1976, Obasanjo completes transition; Ghana: Acheampong 1972, Rawlings 1979, civilian rule within three months, then Rawlings' December 1981 coup.
workedExamples.formula: Framework: transitions succeed when a timetable, reform programme and leadership continuity exist.
workedExamples.substitution: Nigeria kept a timetable and handed back power in 1979; Ghana's short return collapsed when civilian decline resumed.
workedExamples.calculation: Continuity and reform explain Nigeria's success; the failure to halt decline explains Ghana's relapse.
workedExamples.answer: Nigeria moved to civilian rule in 1979 through planned reforms, while Ghana, despite Rawlings' purge of corrupt generals, fell back under military rule in 1981.

commonMistakes: Assuming the military always improved governance; the textbook warns military rulers were just as likely to be corrupt and tyrannical.
Dating Ghana's first coup wrongly; Nkrumah fell in February 1966, and Rawlings first took power in 1979.
Believing the Nigerian civil war began directly at independence; it followed the 1966 coups and the Igbo massacre.
Thinking all French-speaking states were militarized; Guinea, Senegal and Cote d'Ivoire were the notable exceptions.
Confusing Murtala Muhammed with Obasanjo; Muhammed seized power in 1975 and was assassinated in 1976, while Obasanjo restored civilian rule in 1979.
Forgetting that colonial armies existed for internal control, which shaped their post-independence political role.
applications: Discussing how Ethiopia avoided the 1960s coup wave and what institutions gave a government legitimacy.
Drawing lessons for today: restoring moral authority and a clear timetable, as Murtala Muhammed tried in Nigeria in 1975.
Applying the lesson of failed transitions: why election winners must also perform, like Busia who fell to cocoa prices.
Relating food security to politics through 'Operation Feed Yourself' and Ethiopia's own food-import debates.
Debating in class whether a coup can ever be justified against an oppressive elected ruler, using Ghana 1966 as the case.
g12-history-uh7-t2.summary: The post-independence decades were marked by coups and counter-coups because armies inherited for internal control intervened whenever civilian regimes proved inefficient and corrupt. The coup d'etat was the most frequent means of changing government in the 1970s and 1980s, and three tyrannies, those of Bokassa, Idi Amin and Macias Nguema, fell in 1979. Nigeria survived rigged elections, two coups of 1966 and the Biafra war to return to civilian rule in 1979, while Ghana cycled between Nkrumah's fall in 1966 and Rawlings' second seizure of power in December 1981.

g12-history-uh7-t3.overview: This lesson analyses the economy and society of independent Africa: the inherited lack of diversity, the struggle for economic independence against Western domination, and the social problems colonialism planted.
objectives: Explain why inherited colonial economies made independent Africa vulnerable to crisis
Assess the effects of single cash-crop specialization and foreign price fixing
Evaluate the role of international debt and drought in the 1980s and 1990s
Identify countries that achieved substantial economic progress despite dependency
Describe the social impacts of colonialism: disarticulation, urbanization and class formation
g12-history-uh7-t3.simple: Independent Africa inherited economies designed by colonialism, and their major problem was a lack of diversity. Africans had been pushed to produce only raw materials and single cash crops for Europe, with little industrialization; prices were unstable and sometimes fixed in the interest of international monopolies, so a price fall meant crisis and often political instability. The colonialists left a mounting crisis after 85 years of misrule, and international debt and drought stifled development in the 1980s and 1990s; in 1985 twenty-two countries could not feed their populations. Yet Botswana, Algeria, Gabon and Cote d'Ivoire recorded substantial achievements. Colonialism also left dislocated markets and transport, rural-urban migration and slums, new classes dominated by the petty bourgeoisie, and a culture shaken by European influence.
g12-history-uh7-t3.detailed:
An economy made for export. The economic system inherited by the independent states was itself a source of problems, because its major weaknesses were a lack of diversity. Throughout the colonial period Africans were encouraged only to produce raw materials and mineral ores for Europe's industries, and colonial regimes made little effort to establish factories producing manufactured goods. In agriculture, Africans were pushed to specialize in single cash-crop products. The prices of such single products on the world market were not stable, and were sometimes fixed in the metropolitan countries according to the interests of international monopolies. So whenever prices fell, African states faced economic crisis, which in turn became a cause of political instability.

The strain of dependence. European colonial rule left Africa a mounting economic crisis, the end-product of 85 years of colonial misrule. The two major factors stifling African development in the 1980s and 1990s were international debt and drought. Political independence was not matched by economic emancipation: states remained dependent on former colonial masters, receiving financial aid and loans often given with preconditions as well as high interest rates. When loans financed industries, the manufactured goods were expected to be sold to the lending countries at very low prices.

The struggle for economic independence. In economic terms the performance of many countries fell far short of the vision of the anti-colonial leaders. In 1985, 22 countries could not feed their growing populations, and agricultural production declined in the first part of the 1980s. In contrast, some countries recorded substantial achievements, like Botswana, Algeria, Gabon and Cote d'Ivoire, while for others absolute poverty continued to shape daily existence.

Disarticulated production and trade. Colonialism distorted African economic development in many ways. It brought disarticulation in the production of goods, markets, trade, transport and social services. Indigenous market centres were disoriented and eventually killed off as new marketing centres and trade routes exported raw materials to Europe and imported European manufactures. This made African trade mainly export-import oriented and prematurely integrated it into the world market, a premature integration that benefited the advanced European economies and deepened African dependency. Raw materials were shipped to Europe instead of feeding African industries, so there was no organic linkage between agriculture and industry, and the colonial surplus profits were never ploughed back into Africa.

Transport and urban problems. The colonial transport network was limited mainly to railroads and shipping lines, built to dispatch raw materials to the coast, not to link African towns with rural areas. Roads and railroads, such as those in northern Nigeria and the mineral spur lines of Sierra Leone, served exploitation. Social facilities were few and concentrated in urban areas, forcing migration from the countryside and producing rural-urban migration, overcrowding, filthy slum environments, poor hygiene, epidemic disease, social evils and ethnic problems.

Classes and culture. Colonialism created new classes: the bourgeoisie, petty bourgeoisie, proletariat and peasants. The petty bourgeoisie served as the bridge through which colonial masters exploited Africa, which is why at independence this class captured political leadership. Today's power struggles and uneven distribution of wealth reflect this colonial hang-over. Colonialism also challenged traditional lifestyles and culture: Europeans imposed their ways, indigenous religious beliefs were weakened and replaced by Christianity, and Africans were pushed to abandon their own names for European, Christian or Biblical ones.

keyTerms.def: The inherited African economy's dependence on a few raw materials and cash crops rather than varied production.
A single agricultural product grown for export, whose unstable world price could plunge a whole state into crisis.
Big foreign firms whose interests influenced how the prices of African exports were fixed in the metropolitan countries.
One of the two major factors, with drought, that stifled African development in the 1980s and 1990s.
The colonial breaking up of production, markets, trade and transport into disconnected parts serving Europe.
Africa's early absorption into the world market as a raw-material exporter, which deepened dependency.
The class that bridged colonial exploitation and took control of political leadership at independence.
The continuation of foreign domination after independence through economic ties, aid and loans with preconditions.

workedExamples.problem: A country depends on a single cash crop. The world price collapses. Predict the chain of effects using the dependency framework.
workedExamples.given: Prices of single products are unstable and sometimes fixed by international monopolies.
workedExamples.formula: Framework: export dependence converts a world price fall into a national crisis.
workedExamples.substitution: State revenue collapses; the government cannot fund services or repay.
workedExamples.calculation: Economic crisis then becomes a source of political instability, since a government that cannot feed or pay cannot stay legitimate.
workedExamples.answer: The price fall produces fiscal crisis, hardship and political instability, exactly the pattern the lesson identifies in post-independence Africa.

workedExamples.problem: Interpret the 1985 statistic that 22 African countries could not feed their growing populations.
workedExamples.given: Agricultural production declined in the first part of the 1980s; drought and debt stifled development.
workedExamples.formula: Framework: food deficit = the gap between agricultural production and population needs.
workedExamples.substitution: Declining production plus growing population plus drought widened the food gap.
workedExamples.calculation: Twenty-two states appearing on the deficit side shows how far reality fell short of independence hopes.
workedExamples.answer: The statistic measures the depth of the food crisis of the early 1980s, driven by drought, debt and colonial monoculture.

workedExamples.problem: Why did colonial railroads fail to develop Africa, using northern Nigeria and Sierra Leone as evidence?
workedExamples.given: Northern Nigerian railroads and Sierra Leone's mineral spur lines were built to move resources; the network linked raw-material sources to export points, not towns to rural areas.
workedExamples.formula: Framework: infrastructure serves its builder's purpose; judge it by what it connects and for whom.
workedExamples.substitution: The lines connected mines and farms to shipping points for Europe.
workedExamples.calculation: Because the transport served extraction, it left no integrated national network and no farm-to-town linkages after independence.
workedExamples.answer: Colonial infrastructure was built to exploit and export, so it disarticulated rather than integrated the African economy.

commonMistakes: Believing independence automatically brought economic independence; political freedom was not matched by economic emancipation.
Thinking Africa lacked any industry before independence; the point is that colonial regimes deliberately built none.
Blaming African governments alone for the crises; 85 years of colonial misrule created the starting conditions.
Forgetting that loan 'aid' came with preconditions and high interest, not as free development support.
Assuming the petty bourgeoisie were anti-colonial heroes only; they also bridged colonial exploitation and inherited power.
Claiming all African states failed economically; Botswana, Algeria, Gabon and Cote d'Ivoire recorded substantial achievements.
applications: Drawing lessons for Ethiopia: the danger of relying on one or two agricultural exports, as Ghana did with cocoa.
Explaining why African countries push for processing raw materials at home, reversing the colonial export-import pattern.
Analysing Ethiopia's capital city growth against the lesson's warnings about rural-urban migration and slums.
Using the class-formation insight to discuss why elites can perpetuate colonial patterns after the flag changes.
Judging aid contracts: asking who sets prices and conditions, as the textbook shows with loan preconditions.
g12-history-uh7-t3.summary: Independent Africa inherited economies with a fatal lack of diversity, built to export raw materials and single cash crops whose unstable, monopoly-influenced prices turned any fall into crisis and instability. Over 85 years of colonial misrule left disarticulated markets, export-only transport and urban-centered services, and in the 1980s and 1990s international debt and drought, with 22 countries unable to feed themselves by 1985, deepened the crisis. Still, Botswana, Algeria, Gabon and Cote d'Ivoire showed real economic achievement was possible.

pairs.q: What were the two major factors stifling African development in the 1980s and 1990s?
Which countries recorded substantial economic achievements?
pairs.a: Botswana, Algeria, Gabon and Cote d'Ivoire.

pairs.q: Why did trade become 'prematurely integrated' into the world market?
pairs.a: Because colonial trade routes exported raw materials and imported manufactures, making Africa dependent.

pairs.q: Which class captured political leadership at independence and why?
pairs.a: The petty bourgeoisie, because it served as the bridge of colonial exploitation.

questions.explanation: The textbook identifies lack of diversity as the major economic problem.

the crops could not be taxed

questions.q: Name the two major factors that stifled African development in the 1980s and 1990s.
questions.answer: international debt and drought|debt and drought
questions.explanation: International debt and drought were the two major stifling factors.

questions.q: Give the term for the colonial splitting of production, markets, trade and transport into disconnected parts serving Europe.
questions.explanation: Colonialism brought disarticulation in production, markets, trade, transport and social services.

questions.q: In 1985, how many African countries could not feed their growing populations?
questions.explanation: In 1985, 22 countries could not feed their growing populations.

options: Botswana, Algeria, Gabon and Cote d'Ivoire
questions.explanation: Botswana, Algeria, Gabon and Cote d'Ivoire recorded substantial achievements.

questions.q: Railroads in northern Nigeria were built mainly to link towns with rural areas for African development.
questions.explanation: The railroads were built mainly to exploit natural resources and advance colonial presence.

questions.q: Name the class that served as the bridge through which colonial masters exploited Africa and that controlled political leadership at independence.
questions.explanation: The African petty bourgeoisie bridged colonial exploitation and took political power at independence.

questions.q: Why was Africa's integration into the world market called 'premature' and harmful?
options: Because Africa joined too late in history
Because it was export-import oriented and made Africa dependent on the colonial powers
questions.explanation: Premature integration tied Africa's economy to exporting raw materials and importing manufactures, benefiting Europe.

g12-history-uh7-t4.overview: This lesson studies the Cold War in Africa: superpower rivalry from Nasser's Egypt to the Horn of Africa, the violent end of settler colonialism in Angola, Mozambique and Zimbabwe, and the struggle that ended apartheid in South Africa.
objectives: Explain how the USA and the U.S.S.R. competed for influence in Africa
Trace the swings of superpower clients in the Horn of Africa, especially Ethiopia and Somalia
Describe the liberation wars that ended Portuguese rule in Angola and Mozambique
Explain how armed struggle ended white minority rule in Zimbabwe in 1980
Assess the apartheid laws and the nature of the anti-apartheid resistance in South Africa
g12-history-uh7-t4.simple: Africa was a hot spot of Cold War rivalry between the USA and the U.S.S.R. Nasser of Egypt was the first African ruler to seek Soviet arms after the pro-Israel West refused him; Sekou Toure of Guinea followed after 1958, and after Lumumba's murder Mali, Ghana and Algeria leaned to Moscow. Soviet involvement exploded after Portuguese colonialism collapsed, and in the Horn the Soviets switched from Somalia to Ethiopia after the Derg embraced socialism, though Siad Barre expelled them in 1977. Settler colonies had to fight: Angola and Mozambique won independence in 1975 through the MPLA and FRELIMO; ZANU and ZAPU forced Britain's hand so Zimbabwe was born on April 18, 1980. In South Africa apartheid, built on the laws of 1950, met resistance from the ANC until apartheid ended.
g12-history-uh7-t4.detailed:
Superpower rivalry begins. Africa became a hotspot of Cold War rivalry between the USA and the U.S.S.R. The Soviets arrived with a clear anti-imperialist ideology, while the USA at first deferred to its European allies and became visibly involved only when they failed. Neither superpower simply allowed African nationalism to take its course, and African leaders often looked abroad for support against internal factions or external enemies. Gamal Abdel Nasser of Egypt was the first African ruler to develop an interest in Soviet support: the West, pro-Israel, refused to sell him arms, so the Soviets agreed to build the high Aswan Dam and backed Egypt during the Suez crisis of 1956. Sekou Toure of Guinea followed in 1958 when France abandoned his country, and after the assassination of Lumumba and the Congo's ideological split, Mali, Ghana and Algeria sought Soviet support. The Soviets also kept working relations with pro-Western states like Senegal, Nigeria and even monarchic Ethiopia.

The 1960s reversals and the new wave. Throughout the 1960s pro-Soviet leaders were removed: Ben Bella overthrown in 1965, Nkrumah in 1966, Keita in 1968, while Sekou Toure drifted back to France. By decade's end Moscow's most active allies were moderate governments that wanted Soviet arms, and from about 2 million dollars in 1974, Soviet arms sales to Africa rocketed to 3.4 billion dollars in 1979 after the collapse of Portuguese colonialism brought Guinea-Bissau, Mozambique and Angola into the socialist camp. In Mozambique, FRELIMO signed a Treaty of Friendship and Cooperation with the U.S.S.R., which dispatched Bulgarian agronomists, East German engineers, Cuban sugar specialists and Soviet factory managers.

The Horn of Africa. The Horn was perhaps the only part of sub-Saharan Africa where the Soviets had an active strategic interest, lying on the Red Sea route from the Mediterranean to the Indian Ocean and forming the southern periphery of the Middle East. Somalia seemed on its way to becoming the major Soviet client in Black Africa until the Ethiopian revolution reversed this: as the Derg embraced socialism, Moscow changed camps, supplying nearly 2 billion dollars of arms to Ethiopia from 1977 to 1980. Somalia and Ethiopia provided naval bases at Berbera and Dahlak respectively, but Siad Barre expelled the Soviets from Somalia in November 1977 after the enormous arms supply to Ethiopia. Egypt had long been the major recipient of Soviet arms, and Libya's Gaddafi armed his military with Soviet equipment.

The American side. The major U.S. involvement of the 1960s was in Ethiopia: from 1953 to 1977 Ethiopia was a major recipient of American economic and military aid. After the Derg took power in 1974, relations deteriorated and Ethiopia became the number one Soviet arms client in Black Africa, while the U.S. built a better link with Somalia, its policy being to contain Soviet influence. Soviet-American efforts to ease tension in Africa were shaken first by the Angola conflict and then by the Ogaden War. American relations with Egypt changed dramatically under Sadat after Egypt's defeat in the 1973 Yom Kippur War: needing U.S. support in the Sinai, Sadat received massive aid, strengthened by the Camp David Agreement of 1979 with Israel. U.S. relations with Libya stayed hostile; Gaddafi's support for terrorism led Reagan to approve an air strike in 1986, though Gaddafi survived.

Settler colonialism falls: Angola and Mozambique. Liberation movements with significant white settler populations had to fight armed struggles: in Angola from 1961, Portuguese Guinea from 1963 and Mozambique from 1964. The Angolan war was led by the MPLA under Agostino Neto and the Mozambican war by FRELIMO, first led by Eduardo Mondlane until his killing in 1969, then by Samora Machel. Both movements were led and supported by Marxists and enjoyed foreign aid: MPLA from Guinea, FRELIMO from Tanzania and later Zambia. Portugal poured in troops supported by Western white mercenaries and South Africa, spending about 40 percent of government revenue on the armed forces in the early 1970s. The burden produced a domestic political crisis, and in 1973 Guinea unilaterally declared independence, which Portugal recognized as Guinea-Bissau. Mozambique became independent in June 1975 with Machel as first president; in the same year Sao Tome and the Cape Verde islands also became independent. Angola's independence was arranged for November 1975, but Portugal's hasty withdrawal produced a power struggle between the MPLA and Jonas Savimbi's UNITA; in early 1976 the Angolan People's Republic was established under Neto, with UNITA continuing guerrilla war for years.

Zimbabwe. Southern Rhodesia entrenched white rule: a June 1969 referendum approved a constitution enshrining power in the white minority, and on March 2, 1970 Rhodesia declared itself a republic. The banned movements ZAPU and ZANU operated from exile in Zambia and Mozambique, while the 1971 negotiations produced a third party, the United African National Council, led by Bishop Abel Muzorewa, able to organize inside. Violence intensified after a ZANU attack in December 1972; the Zambia-Rhodesia border closed in 1973, and Mozambique's independence in 1975 gave ZANU a base linked to the FRELIMO government. In 1976 Nkomo of ZAPU and Mugabe of ZANU formed the Patriotic Front, backed by the frontline states, and by 1979 the pressure forced Ian Smith to accept an internal settlement. The UANC won the April 1979 election and adopted the name Zimbabwe, but the war could not end without the PF; Britain retook control briefly, and in the February 1980 elections ZANU won 57 of the 80 Black seats, ZAPU 20 and UANC 3. Mugabe became the first prime minister as Zimbabwe achieved recognized independence on April 18, 1980.

Apartheid and its fall. After the Second World War the Afrikaner National Party, fearing black majority power and the spread of African liberation, won the 1948 election and fortified segregation as apartheid, 'separateness', treating Blacks as aliens in their own land. The Population Registration Act of 1950 classified everyone by race, dividing Blacks into groups like Zulu, Xhosa, Tswana, Venda and Sotho; the Group Areas Act of 1950 assigned where each race could live and work, with separate buses, schools and public places, and labour unions were banned; the Bantu Education Act of 1953 kept Blacks out of missionary schools and taught their inferiority. Resistance organized under the African National Congress (ANC), founded in 1912 and led by figures like Nelson Mandela, Oliver Tambo and Walter Sisulu. On March 21, 1960 police massacred 69 peaceful demonstrators and wounded 180 at Sharpeville near Johannesburg, a turning point; the regime banned the ANC and PAC, Britain and the USA vetoed UN sanctions, ANC president Albert Luthuli won the 1961 Nobel Peace Prize, and South Africa left the Commonwealth, declaring itself a republic in 1961. The ANC then formed its armed wing, Umkhonto we Sizwe (Spear of the Nation), which attacked regime positions in 1963; in the same year Mandela, Walter Sisulu, Govan Mbeki and six others were sentenced to life imprisonment. Strikes by Natal workers in the early 1970s forced the lifting of some union bans, the Black Consciousness movement restored black dignity and self-reliance, and in the early 1980s Blacks boycotted white-owned shops and schools in the Eastern Cape and Transvaal. After long years of confinement Nelson Mandela was freed and later served as the first president of post-apartheid South Africa.

keyTerms.def: The rivalry between the USA and the U.S.S.R. after 1945, in which Africa became a battleground for influence.
The Popular Movement for the Liberation of Angola, led by Agostino Neto, which fought Portugal from 1961.
The Front for the Liberation of Mozambique, led by Eduardo Mondlane and later Samora Machel; it won independence in June 1975.
Jonas Savimbi's movement that fought the MPLA government in guerrilla war after Angola's independence.
The 1976 alliance of Nkomo's ZAPU and Mugabe's ZANU that pressured Smith's Rhodesia toward settlement.
South Africa's racist policy of 'separateness' that treated the black majority as aliens in their own land.
The Spear of the Nation, the armed wing of the ANC created for armed struggle; it attacked regime positions in 1963.
The movement that restored black dignity and urged Black South Africans to free themselves without white help.

workedExamples.problem: Explain the reversal of superpower positions in the Horn of Africa between 1974 and 1978.
workedExamples.given: Somalia was the coming Soviet client; the Derg took power in Ethiopia in 1974; from 1977 to 1980 Ethiopia received nearly 2 billion dollars of arms; Siad Barre expelled the Soviets in November 1977.
workedExamples.formula: Framework: superpowers choose clients by ideology and strategic interest, and switch them when clients switch.
workedExamples.substitution: As the Derg embraced socialism, Moscow saw a new client; as it armed Ethiopia, Somalia's value vanished.
workedExamples.calculation: Soviet strategy in the Red Sea route preferred the larger client, so weapons followed ideology: bases and arms shifted to Ethiopia, and Somalia turned to the USA.
workedExamples.answer: Cold War alliances were deals, not friendships: ideology moved Ethiopia into the Soviet camp, which forced Somalia out and reoriented U.S. policy in the Horn.

workedExamples.problem: Read the figures: Soviet arms sales to sub-Saharan Africa grew from about 2 million dollars in 1974 to 3.4 billion dollars in 1979. What does a historian conclude?
workedExamples.given: The collapse of Portuguese colonialism in 1975 brought Guinea-Bissau, Mozambique and Angola into the socialist camp.
workedExamples.formula: Framework: a sudden rise in military supplies marks the arrival of new clients and new conflicts.
workedExamples.substitution: The jump of over a thousand times coincides exactly with Angola, Mozambique and Guinea-Bissau joining the socialist camp.
workedExamples.calculation: Data of this scale indicates a strategic commitment, not routine trade; Angola's war with UNITA required steady Soviet logistic support.
workedExamples.answer: The figures show that the fall of Portuguese settler colonialism in 1975 opened a new, heavily militarized phase of the Cold War in Africa.

workedExamples.problem: Why did Sharpeville (March 21, 1960) become a turning point of the anti-apartheid struggle?
workedExamples.given: Police killed 69 and wounded 180 peaceful demonstrators near Johannesburg; the ANC and PAC were banned; the UN condemned; Britain and the USA vetoed sanctions; Luthuli won the 1961 Nobel Peace Prize.
workedExamples.formula: Framework: a turning point is an event that changes both the state's tactics and the movement's methods.
workedExamples.substitution: The massacre exposed the regime's brutality, forced bans on the movements, and pushed the ANC from non-violence to armed struggle through Umkhonto we Sizwe.
workedExamples.calculation: Repression plus international condemnation meant the cost of the status quo rose for everyone, so the struggle entered a new phase in and after 1960.
workedExamples.answer: Sharpeville radicalized the struggle: the regime banned the movements by force, the ANC took up arms, and the world began to judge apartheid a moral question.

commonMistakes: Believing African states stayed neutral like the Cold War blocs; African leaders actively sought external patrons for their own struggles.
Reversing the Horn switch: Ethiopia became the Soviet client after 1974, while the USA moved closer to Somalia.
Forgetting that Siad Barre expelled the Soviets in November 1977, so Soviet-Somali ties ended before Ethiopia's arms deal.
Thinking Mozambique's independence came before its war; FRELIMO fought from 1964 to 1975.
Mistaking UNITA for an anti-colonial movement; it fought the independent MPLA government after 1975.
Assuming apartheid began in the 1960s; the National Party entrenched it from its 1948 election victory.
Believing sanctions succeeded at once; Britain and the USA vetoed the proposed UN economic sanctions.
applications: Linking Ethiopia's own history: the 1953-1977 U.S. relationship, the Derg's turn to Moscow and the 1977 Ogaden War context.
Tracing Mandela's Ethiopian connection: the ANC received training in Addis Ababa in the anti-apartheid struggle.
Using the Zimbabwe case (57 of 80 seats in 1980) to practise reading election results as evidence of legitimacy.
Comparing liberation movements' foreign support with today's debates on foreign interference in African conflicts.
Discussing how apartheid's legal architecture, registration and group areas laws, warns against any racialized Ethiopian politics.
g12-history-uh7-t4.summary: The Cold War divided Africa as both superpowers armed competing clients, with dramatic swings in the Horn where Moscow exchanged Somalia for the Derg's Ethiopia, which received about 2 billion dollars of arms by 1980, while Siad Barre expelled the Soviets in 1977. Settler-ruled territories won freedom by arms: Angola and Mozambique in 1975 through the MPLA and FRELIMO, and Zimbabwe on April 18, 1980 after ZANU and ZAPU broke white Rhodesia's hold. In South Africa, apartheid, legislated in 1950, was resisted by the ANC through non-violence, the Sharpeville turning point of 1960, armed Umkhonto we Sizwe fighters and Black Consciousness until apartheid finally collapsed.

g12-history-uh7-t5.overview: This lesson follows Pan-Africanism from its origins among black peoples of the Americas through the Manchester Conference of 1945, the founding of the OAU in Addis Ababa in 1963 with Ethiopia's mediation, and its transformation into the African Union in 2002.
objectives: Explain the origin and meaning of Pan-Africanism among black peoples of the Americas
Compare the ideas of W.E.B. Du Bois and Marcus Garvey
Evaluate what made the 1945 Manchester Conference a landmark
Describe the Casablanca and Monrovia groups and Ethiopia's role in founding the OAU
Assess the successes and failures of the OAU and the transformation into the African Union
g12-history-uh7-t5.simple: Pan-Africanism is the desire for African unity and the brotherhood of all black peoples; the word 'pan' means 'all' in Greek. It began outside Africa among blacks of the Americas resisting white racism. A Trinidadian, H. Sylvester Williams, organized the first Pan-African Conference in London in 1900; Du Bois, the Father of Pan-Africanism, argued for rights in host countries, while Garvey's 1914 Universal Negro Improvement Association preached return to Africa. The Fifth Conference at Manchester in 1945 first brought continental Africans like Nkrumah and Kenyatta and demanded independence. The Casablanca and Monrovia groups competed over the shape of unity until Emperor Haile Selassie I united them at Addis Ababa, where 32 states founded the OAU in May 1963. Criticized as a dictators' club for its non-interference, the OAU was replaced by the African Union, inaugurated at Durban in July 2002 after the Sirte Declaration of 1999.
g12-history-uh7-t5.detailed:
What Pan-Africanism is. Pan-Africanism is an expression of the desire for African unity and of a sense of brotherhood among all black peoples of African origin in Africa, North and South America, and the West Indies. It originated and developed outside the African continent, among black people of African origin in the Americas: Afro-Americans in the USA and the Caribbean, made homeless by eviction from their countries of origin, sought equality with other races and justice for black people. At first it was the resistance of black people against white racism; many saw Africa as a continent where black people lived free and happy, a vision of Africa without frontiers that gave birth to the idea of the United States of Africa. The word 'pan' means 'all' in Greek, so Pan-Africanism means bringing Africans together.

The congresses. The first organized expression was the First Pan-African Conference in London in 1900, organized by H. Sylvester Williams of Trinidad and Tobago, attended mainly by people from America and the West Indies. Before 1945 four conferences were held, dominated by two great figures: William Du Bois (1868-1963), the African-American scholar called the Father of Pan-Africanism, and Marcus Garvey (1887-1940), a Jamaican who moved to the USA and founded the Universal Negro Improvement Association in 1914. The two criticized each other: Du Bois believed blacks outside Africa should struggle for rights in their host countries, while Garvey insisted their future lay in returning to the mother continent through his 'Back to Africa Movement'.

Manchester 1945. The Fifth Pan-African Conference, held in Manchester in 1945, was a landmark: for the first time Africans from the continent participated and the independence of Africa was on the agenda. Its participants included future leaders like Kwame Nkrumah of Ghana and Jomo Kenyatta of Kenya, and it declared that Africans would resort to violent means unless independence was seriously considered. Its resolutions became the slogan that rallied Africans to the struggle for political independence and laid the foundation for the emergence of a continental organization. After 1945 African leaders divided over whether to create a single politically united Africa; some, like President Julius Nyerere of Tanzania and President Nkrumah, saw creating strong nation-states as the first step toward a larger United States of Africa, while others insisted Pan-Africanism must come only after each country's independence so as not to weaken the sovereignty of the new states.

Two blocs and the birth of the OAU. Two blocs competed before 1963. The Casablanca group (founded 1961: Ghana, Algeria, Guinea, Morocco, Egypt, Mali and Libya) favored an immediate political union of African states through federation. The Monrovian group (Ethiopia, Nigeria, Liberia, Sierra Leone, Togo, Tunisia, Congo Kinshasa and Somalia) favored first economic integration, followed by gradual, step-by-step political integration. The process of forming a continental organization had begun around 1958, and Emperor Haile Selassie I, though Ethiopia belonged to the Monrovian group, invited both contending blocs to Addis Ababa and convinced their leaders to compromise. The OAU was founded in May 1963 in Addis Ababa by 32 African states signing its Charter, and its first conference was held there; since 1963 Addis Ababa has served as the headquarters of the OAU and then the African Union. The OAU's primary aims were to coordinate and intensify cooperation for a better life for African peoples, to defend the sovereignty, territorial integrity and independence of member states, and to eradicate all forms of colonialism and white minority rule; it also sought to ensure human rights, raise living standards, and settle disputes peacefully and diplomatically. A Liberation Committee was established to aid independence movements, and the organization kept neutral in the Cold War so its members would not be re-controlled by outside powers.

Ethiopia's role and the OAU's record. Ethiopia, the only African country never colonized after its 1896 victory at Adwa, was a role model for Africans and the entire black race, and Haile Selassie can be taken as a father figure of the OAU. Ethiopia gave military training to the ANC leader Nelson Mandela in Addis Ababa, supported the South African struggle against apartheid, and under Mengistu Haile Mariam trained thousands of Zimbabwean freedom fighters. The OAU helped African countries under colonial rule to achieve independence; its members acted together in the UN in the anti-colonial struggle, provided firearms, training and military bases for liberation movements, backed the anti-apartheid and Zimbabwean struggles, and even barred South African aircraft from African airspace; it also founded the African Development Bank to finance development projects. But it had failures: it could not stop the civil wars in Nigeria and Angola, and its policy of non-interference made it silent when member governments violated human rights, so it failed even to condemn Idi Amin. Critics called it a 'Dictators' Club', and point to Morocco's departure in November 1984 in protest against the admission of the Saharawi Arab Democratic Republic in 1982, plus the absence of any enforcement agency or military wing.

From the OAU to the AU. On September 9, 1999, African Heads of State and Government met at an OAU summit in Sirte, Libya, and issued the Sirte Declaration, calling for a new continental organization to replace the OAU, driven by the desire to hasten African integration and help Africa face the adverse effects of globalization. The African Union was officially inaugurated in July 2002 in Durban, South Africa. Unlike the OAU, the AU claimed to be a forum of the entire African peoples, with organs modelled on the UN: the Assembly of Heads of State and Government, the Executive Council, the Permanent Representatives Committee, the Specialized Technical Committees, the Peace and Security Council and the African Union Commission. It added the Pan-African Parliament, the Economic, Social and Cultural Council (ECOSOCC), human rights institutions like the African Commission and Court on Human and Peoples' Rights, the African Union Advisory Board on Corruption and the Committee of Experts on the Rights and Welfare of the Child, and it aims to establish continental monetary institutions: a central bank, an investment bank and a continental monetary fund.

keyTerms.def: The desire for African unity and the brotherhood of all black peoples of African origin; 'pan' means 'all' in Greek.
The Pan-Africanist ideal of one federated African state, which divided Casablanca and Monrovia blocs.
The Trinidadian who organized the First Pan-African Conference in London in 1900.
Garvey's programme, promoted by the Universal Negro Improvement Association of 1914, urging blacks abroad to return to Africa.
The 1961 bloc of Ghana, Algeria, Guinea, Morocco, Egypt, Mali and Libya favouring immediate political federation.
The bloc of Ethiopia, Nigeria, Liberia, Sierra Leone, Togo, Tunisia, Congo Kinshasa and Somalia favouring economic integration first, then gradual political union.
The controversial OAU policy of not intervening in member states' internal affairs, which silenced it on human rights abuses.
The declaration of September 9, 1999 at Sirte, Libya calling for the African Union to replace the OAU.

workedExamples.problem: Compare the Casablanca and Monrovian groups using the framework of gradualism versus immediate union.
workedExamples.given: Casablanca (1961): Ghana, Algeria, Guinea, Morocco, Egypt, Mali, Libya wanted an immediate political union through federation; Monrovian: Ethiopia, Nigeria, Liberia, Sierra Leone, Togo, Tunisia, Congo Kinshasa, Somalia wanted economic integration first, then step-by-step political union.
workedExamples.formula: Framework: organizations of union differ on sequence (political first or economic first) and on speed (immediate or gradual).
workedExamples.substitution: Casablanca puts political federation ahead of everything; Monrovia prices sovereignty and economy first.
workedExamples.calculation: Ethiopia sat in the Monrovian camp but its emperor used that position to broker unity rather than deepen the split.
workedExamples.answer: The split was about sequence and sovereignty; Haile Selassie's mediation merged both positions into the OAU founded at Addis Ababa in May 1963.

workedExamples.problem: Judge the OAU's performance using the evidence for success and failure.
workedExamples.given: Successes: liberation support with arms, training and bases; joint UN action; South African aircraft barred from African skies; the African Development Bank. Failures: silence under non-interference, no condemnation of Idi Amin, no enforcement agency, Morocco's exit in 1984.
workedExamples.formula: Framework: evaluate an organization on mandate fulfilment, enforcement capacity and member conduct.
workedExamples.substitution: The OAU met its anti-colonial mandate fully but its human rights and peace aims failed.
workedExamples.calculation: Because it lacked an enforcement agency and a military wing and hid behind non-interference, successes in liberation were not matched by successes in governance.
workedExamples.answer: The OAU succeeded in ending colonialism and white minority rule but failed to build peace and rights inside its own member states.

workedExamples.problem: What transformed the Fifth Pan-African Conference of 1945 into the institutional chain that produced the AU?
workedExamples.given: Manchester 1945 had continental Africans like Nkrumah and Kenyatta and raised independence; the OAU formed in May 1963; the Sirte Declaration in 1999; the AU inaugurated at Durban in 2002.
workedExamples.formula: Framework: movements become institutions when ideas gain structures and dates.
workedExamples.substitution: The 1945 demand for independence led to 1963's continental organization and then to 2002's deeper union.
workedExamples.calculation: Each step kept the same goal, unity, while upgrading its instrument: from congress, to intergovernmental OAU, to the integrated peoples' Union.
workedExamples.answer: Manchester supplied the idea and leaders, Addis Ababa in 1963 supplied the institution, and Sirte in 1999 renewed it as the African Union of 2002.

commonMistakes: Thinking Pan-Africanism was born in Africa; it originated outside the continent, among black peoples of the Americas.
Confusing Du Bois and Garvey's programmes; Du Bois sought rights in host countries, Garvey preached return to Africa.
Dating the first conference to 1945; the first Pan-African Conference was held in London in 1900.
Reversing the two blocs' positions; it was the Casablanca group that wanted immediate federation, not the Monrovian group.
Claiming the OAU had an army and enforcement power; it had neither, which limited it to diplomacy.
Forgetting Ethiopia's decisive role in bridging the blocs and hosting the OAU since 1963.
Assuming the AU appeared without decision; it followed the Sirte Declaration of September 9, 1999.
applications: Explaining Ethiopia's soft power: Addis Ababa as the capital of Africa, hosting the OAU and AU since May 1963.
Tracing Ethiopia's solidarity history: training Nelson Mandela in Addis Ababa and thousands of Zimbabwean fighters.
Using the 1896 victory at Adwa to explain Ethiopia's moral authority among African nationalist leaders.
Analysing the shift from non-interference to the AU's Peace and Security Council, and what it promises for African conflicts.
Applying integration logic to today's African free-trade debates: economic integration first, as the Monrovian group argued.
Judging Ethiopian aspirations within Pan-Africanism: unity that protects national sovereignty, the Monrovian position Ethiopia defended.
g12-history-uh7-t5.summary: Pan-Africanism, born among blacks of the Americas and organized from the 1900 London conference through the landmark Manchester meeting of 1945, supplied the idea and leaders for African unity. Haile Selassie I bridged the Casablanca and Monrovia blocs, and 32 states founded the OAU at Addis Ababa in May 1963, which led the anti-colonial struggle but fell short on rights and enforcement, earning the label 'Dictators' Club'. Through the Sirte Declaration of 1999 the OAU was transformed into the African Union, inaugurated at Durban in July 2002 with organs reaching from the Peace and Security Council to the Pan-African Parliament.

questions.q: The term 'pan' in Pan-Africanism means 'all' in which language?
questions.explanation: 'Pan' is Greek for 'all', so Pan-Africanism means bringing Africans together.

questions.q: Who organized the First Pan-African Conference held in London in 1900?
questions.explanation: The Trinidadian H. Sylvester Williams organized the first conference in 1900.

questions.q: Which Pan-African leader is referred to as the Father of Pan-Africanism?
questions.answer: dubois|du bois|william dubois|w e b dubois
questions.explanation: The African-American scholar William Du Bois is called the Father of Pan-Africanism.

questions.q: Marcus Garvey organized the 'Back to Africa Movement' through the Universal Negro Improvement Association.
questions.explanation: Garvey founded the UNIA in 1914 to promote his Back to Africa Movement.

questions.q: What made the Fifth Pan-African Conference of 1945 different from the previous conferences?
options: For the first time Africans from the continent participated and the issue of African independence was raised
It rejected any use of violence
questions.explanation: Manchester 1945 was the first with continental African participants, including Nkrumah and Kenyatta, and it demanded independence.

questions.q: The Organization of African Unity was founded in May 1963 by:
questions.explanation: 32 African states signed the OAU Charter at Addis Ababa in May 1963.

questions.q: Which group favored an immediate political union of African states through federation?
questions.explanation: The Casablanca group of 1961 favored immediate political federation.

questions.q: Name the two contending blocs over African unity before 1963.
questions.answer: casablanca and monrovian|casablanca group and monrovian group|casablanca and monrovia
questions.explanation: The Casablanca and Monrovian groups competed over the structure of African unity.

questions.q: Because of its policy of non-interference, the OAU kept silent when member governments violated the human rights of their citizens.
questions.explanation: Non-interference made the OAU silent, so it failed even to condemn Idi Amin.

questions.q: The Sirte Declaration of September 9, 1999 called for:
options: admitting South Africa to the OAU
establishing the African Union to replace the OAU
a military wing for the OAU
questions.explanation: The Sirte Declaration in Libya called for a new continental organization, the African Union.

questions.q: Why did Morocco leave the OAU in November 1984?
questions.answer: protest against the admission of the sahara ar amp democratic republic|opposition to western sahara|disagreement over the sahara ar amp democratic republic|protest over western sahara
questions.explanation: Morocco left in protest against the OAU's 1982 admission of the Saharawi Arab Democratic Republic.
